facts.statement: Gurilynia is classified as a genus of enantiornithine birds.
facts.quote: Gurilynia is a genus of enantiornithine birds.

facts.statement: Gurilynia lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 70 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: It lived during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, between 70 and 66 mya.

facts.statement: Fossils of Gurilynia were found at the Gurilyn Tsav locality in the Nemegt Formation of south Gobi, Mongolia.
facts.quote: Gurilynia is known from fragmentary fossils found at the Gurilyn Tsav locality of the Nemegt Formation in south Gobi, Mongolia.

facts.statement: Only one species, Gurilynia nessovi, is known from this genus.
facts.quote: One species is known, G. nessovi.

facts.statement: Gurilynia nessovi is the largest known Mesozoic bird from Mongolia, reaching a length of 53 cm, a hip height of 23.2 cm, and a weight of 2.1 kg.
facts.quote: This specimen indicates the largest Mongolian Mesozoic bird, with a length of 53 cm, hip height of 23.2 cm, and weight of 2.1 kg.

facts.statement: The humeral head of Gurilynia is approximately 29 mm wide.
facts.quote: The humeral head is around 29 mm wide.

facts.statement: All known Gurilynia fossils are housed in the collection of the Paleontological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
facts.quote: All three fossils are in the collection of the Paleontological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

facts.statement: Gurilynia belongs to the family Enantiornithidae.
Gurilynia nessovi is the type species of the genus Gurilynia.
The time range for Gurilynia is the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Gurilynia nessovi provides evidence that large Enantiornithes existed in both Central Asia and the Americas during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Kurochkin also adds that G. nessovi demonstrates that there were large Enantiornithids in Central Asia as well as the Americas at the end of the Cretaceous.
